newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Parties and rebels scorn Burundi political changes.
newsitem.headline: Parties and rebels scorn Burundi political changes.

text.p: Burundi's rebels and main Tutsi and Hutu parties dismissed the lifting of political bans by military ruler Pierre Buyoya on Friday as a bid to loosen the grip of sanctions.
Exiled political spokesmen for the majority Hutu tribe said it was in any case too dangerous for them to return to the Tutsi-run capital, Bujumbura.
Charles Mukasi, leader of the Tutsi-dominated Uprona party, said parliament had no real power before Buyoya took over in a July 25 coup by the Tutsi-dominated army and it would remain powerless.
Buyoya's military-apppointed government announced late on Thursday it was immediately lifting bans on all political parties and the national assembly imposed during the coup.

"Lifting the ban on parliament is a cosmetic change simply designed to please (Julius) Nyerere," Mukasi told Reuters. The former Tanzanian president is the main mediator on Burundi and master-minded sanctions imposed by regional states on July 31.

"They are restoring an institution that was incapable of functioning. Power is held by the government," added Mukasi, a Hutu. He said he was pleased by the lifting of the ban on political parties as Uprona had been unfairly penalised.

If genuine, the changes meet two of the three conditions set by regional African leaders before they would remove the embargo clamped on the landlocked country. The third condition is unconditional peace negotiations among all parties including Hutu rebels.

"They don't mean anything. Constitutional rule has not been restored," said Innocent Nimpagaritse, Africa representative for the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), the political wing of the main Hutu rebel group.
"Buyoya is illegal. Most members of parliament are in exile. This just won't work. All he wants is sanctions to be removed."
"Since the beginning we have said we want to force the army to negotiate. CNDD will continue its military operations until the mono-ethnic army accepts to negotiate without conditions."
In Dar es Salaam, a spokesman for exiled members of the Hutu -dominated Frodebu party said the changes amounted to nothing.

"There's no change. How do you restore the national assembly without restoring the constitution," said Niyonzima Hermenegilde in the Tanzanian capital. "He wants to deceive regional heads of state to diminish sanctions."
"The most important thing for Burundi is peace. He hasn't said anything about negotiating with CNDD," said Hermenegilde, adding Frodebu party chairman Jean Minani held the same views.
But at the German ambassador's residence in Bujumbura where he took refuge during the coup, Leonce Ngendakumana, the Hutu president of the national assembly, welcomed the concessions.
"We will participate on condition it is the old national assembly and there are no named deputies," he told Reuters, adding he wanted to see talks between the government and rebels.
Frodebu swept Burundi's last free elections in 1993, winning a big majority in parliament. But most Frodebu MPs are either in exile or underground and some have been assassinated.
U.S. embassy officials said ousted Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, holed up at the U.S. ambassador's residence in Bujumbura since the coup, could not be reached for any comment.
